problem: The sentence is broken and unreadable: 'A column with λ 7.4.' The comparison sign and the whole second half are missing, so the student never learns what happens for λ below 89, which is the main point of the section.
fix: A column with λ > 89 buckles elastically and Euler applies. A column with λ < 89 reaches the yield stress before it buckles, so Euler predicts a stress the material cannot carry; such a column is short or stocky and must be designed by the Rankine-Gordon formula or a column curve (see 7.4).

problem: Euler is valid up to the proportional limit, not the yield stress. Saying the proportional limit is 'taken as the yield stress' quietly shifts the limit upward; for mild steel the proportional limit sits below yield, so the cut-off slenderness is nearer 80-85 than 89 in real design.
fix: Euler remains valid only while σ_cr stays below the proportional limit. In simple calculations this limit is often taken as the yield stress σ_c, which is slightly unconservative: it gives λ ≈ 89 for σ_c = 250 MPa, while a proportional limit below yield would give a larger cut-off slenderness.
